en: A hero born of a noble father,
Who subdued the whole wide world.
He won Kongurbay over with his words,
Revealing what a profound champion he was;
He was about to draw the fatal line.
Such is a true hero when you behold him—
Your gray wolf was about to stage his feat.
Moving between them, that crafty man
Had marked out the city of Beijing;
He was about to bring down upon it
A calamity no mortal had ever seen.
Setting the caravan in motion and leading the migration,
He would cunningly avenge himself on your Prince Kalcha;
Such was the falcon’s intention:
To pursue him to the bitter end
And finish Kalcha by cutting off his head.
He meant to inflict surpassing torment
And avenge the noble
Prince Almambet.
If his strength sufficed, he would attack
And cast Alööke Khan’s Kongurbay
Flat upon his back.
The nimble-born lion-warrior,
A blazing fire wherever he turned,
Would make whole armies give way when he struck,
And burn every enemy he faced.
Could the valor of Almambet’s warrior son
Truly be so great?
He was both a hero and a lion,
One who subdued the whole wide world,
And they called that champion Külchoro.
Resourceful by birth, Külchoro
Displayed his cunning;
He won over the Manchu khan Ezkara
And Alööke’s Kongurbay,
Persuading Alööke with his words,
And displaying his lionhearted courage—
The warrior among spear-wielders—
He has commanding presence too,
The resourceful companion
Has strength as well.
Eloquent of tongue and masterful in speech—
Can there be another man like this companion?
Would it be right to speak so
Of that wretched companion?
Immeasurably swift,
The keen and valiant companion.
His prowess is beyond measure;
Named the companion of companions,
He has hardened himself on blood.
Among all the heroes
Known by ear and seen by eye,
He has won renown as Külchoro.
A mighty-born lion of a companion,
Perfect in every limb.
Have you ever heard
Of a hero who could annihilate
Not only China, but the whole world?
His forefathers, who chased white deer
And herded them like cattle,
Were the ancestors
Of the companion who made battlefields his domain.
They chased blue deer and herded them like cattle;
This Külchoro, now lying buried,
Made every place he sought his domain.
From the aged patriarch
Khan Koshoy of Katagan he received a blessing;
Joining all twelve limbs in strength,
This incorrigible companion
Came to be called the bloodthirsty warrior.
Ninety beasts were slaughtered for his feast,
And he was granted the name of Lion.
His quality as a swift steed was plain:
Beneath him was the racehorse Buurul,
And even in old age this leopard
Could still deceive the Kalmyk.
He is Semetey’s kinsman,
One who can never drink his fill of blood,
Another lion of the Kyrgyz.
Orphaned of his father,
Born without ever seeing his face—
Such was the companion’s fate,
Yet he stirred turmoil throughout the world.
Wearing an amulet around his neck,
He was raised by Kanykey;
They kicked and frolicked together like foals,
And, like true brothers,
Contended for milk at the same breast.
These words are no falsehood:
If you ask who the boy is,
He is bloodthirsty Semetey’s companion.
And Semetey’s affair stood thus:
The Kyrgyz and Chinese, the two peoples,
Hurried to declare that they had made peace,
While between them Buurul reared and plunged
As though his master had been slain.
They made him pace back and forth,
And drove all the Kyrgyz and Chinese
Into frantic commotion,
As though a slaughter had struck them.
Amid them Külchoro
Rode forth as an envoy,
With all his weapons made ready,
And a sheathless sword at his waist.
Like a cloud returning with rain,
Wrath spread across his face.
Ah, thick-armed and stone-hearted,
A powerfully built daredevil,
When vast armies closed in combat,
He never opened his flank in fear;
When he entered the fray,
He crushed men to earth like rabbits.
The boy was surpassingly noble,
And he was a lion besides,
A wise and discerning hero
Who knew every stratagem of the foe.
He was a true hero as well.
This one too was a blood-drinking warrior,
A champion of the Kyrgyz.
He was a lion by creation,
Whose like did not exist in all the world.
When the storm came, he let no wind pass,
But stood as a walled and fortified stronghold;
The champion of the mighty Kyrgyz
Was a banner planted on the heights.
This lion-born, valiant companion,
When unleashed against a challenging foe,
Became calamity and turmoil itself.
Among round-headed mortals
Another such could never be born.
Broad-chested and firm as stone,
Such was the comely companion;
Let us hear the answer
That fulfilled bloodthirsty Semetey’s wish.
The bridle fastened to his horse,
He who remained six months in the womb
After the death of his father, the khan’s posthumous hope.
Across passes, valleys, and springs,
Never sated by drinking blood,
Never sparing a life once he attacked—
He too was one of the fearsome ones.
Hardened by constantly spilling blood,
To every mortal who had heard of him
The poor man was known as the subduer of women.
His fortune was complete;
He was a lion upheld by providence.
What matter if bloodthirsty was his name?
Save that he was the son of Manas,
Külchoro was a spear-cast
More valiant than Semetey.
Powerful in cunning and mighty in stature,
Both champion wrestler and lion,
He was an exceptional hero who knew
Every stratagem of his enemy.
His valor was extraordinary,
And this furious companion’s
Strength was beyond measure.
He spurred the gray steed that flew like a cloud,
Making it bound in excitement;
Arbuurul, greatest of beasts,
Grew wildly restive again and again.
Riding Buurul, he made him plunge,
Driving the peerless racehorse
Into a frenzy of rearing.
He wore golden greaves reaching the ridge of his boots,
With embroidered trouser cuffs.
The riding breeches Kanykey had made
Shimmered at the hems.
Akkelte, left by your champion Manas,
Flashed across his broad back.
Ah, the thundering madman
Girded on a silver-mounted belt,
Smiling as he spoke and struck fear.
Taking a steel axe in his hand,
He mounted and rode between the two sides.
On the farther side stood Semetey;
The companion spoke these words to them,
Then made Buurul prance proudly
And rode up, that fierce man.
Semetey, Bakay, and Sarykan,
With his heroic elder Kanchoro,
Came and offered counsel.
“My two elders, Sarykan and Bakay,
You old men are standing here.
My bloodthirsty elder Semetey,
With brave Kanchoro at your head,
All of you are standing here.
In wisdom and strategy
I have never been found wanting.
I deceived Alööke’s son Kongurbay,
The Manchu khan of the Kalmaks,
Calling him my kinsman,
And led him onto the road.
Ezkara and the aged Kalmyk—
Like men already struck by slaughter,
I artfully deceived them all
And displayed my lionhearted nature.
The infidel son of Kalday,
The warrior Khan Kongurbay,
I deceived and brought around to my word.
I approached him from the Kirma side,
Claiming I had fled from the Kyrgyz,
And deceived him by saying I was Chinese.
‘Our first ancestor was Chylaba,’ I said,
And invoked his ancestral spirit.
The blue-gray-bearded Chinese warrior
And his interpreter Ezkara—
Such was the state of those accursed men;
I deceived every one of them.
My princely elders, my sultans,
I have shown you my resourcefulness
And delivered the Kalmyk hero Kongurbay
Into your hands.
Torment him as you would a sheep;
Do not spare the Kalmyk’s life—
Cut off his head.
Drag him through the people
And expose him to the Danggits.
Let the black blood flowing from within him
Cure the pain in your heart,
Heal the sickness inside you—
Scoop it up by the handful and swallow!
May the place that aches be soothed;
Once you capture Kongurbay,
Alas, my lionhearted elder,
May your clouded eyes open wide.
May your scorched heart
Be calmed as though sprinkled with water,
And may your painful yearning be healed;
May the grave of the Kalmyk
Who subjugated the whole world be opened.
Send Ezkara into the grave,
Displaying your valor to the utmost,
And make the few, long-suffering Kyrgyz
Rejoice and laugh.
Let us fulfill the wishes
Of this nation left desolate;
Let us distribute gold by the foot and worldly treasure,
Saying, ‘This is the blood-price of ten generations
Of your forefathers.’
Let us set every hero’s heart at ease,
Make these Kyrgyz rich,
And exalt our valor.
Let us kill the champions
Of the red-tasseled Chinese,
Then rest, my precious elder.
Let us crush the finest men
Of the stone-buttoned Chinese
And make merry.
Let us capture the strongest
Of the jacketed Manchus
And cure every brooding sorrow.
By calling the Chinese my kin,
I planted open hostility
Right beside them.
I sowed a feud that will bring disaster,
